full_text:
Universities should go back to traditional exams and in-person presentations to grade students after lecturers complained that AI has made it “close to impossible” to assess coursework, according to an investigation by England’s higher education regulator.

The Office for Students (OfS) said the credibility of degrees from England’s universities was under threat from the prolific use of AI in essays, dissertations and “open book” exams, with students reporting that their peers boasted of using AI undetected by staff.

The regulator warned universities and other higher education institutions that failing to design “valid and reliable measures of students’ knowledge and skills” to combat AI could breach their conditions of registration and lead to sanctions being imposed.

Josh Fleming, the director of strategy and delivery at the OfS, said AI use in higher education “presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students’ learning and institutions’ ability to assess them”.

Fleming added: “We need to see far greater efforts to tackle these risks, including far greater use of AI-free assessment.

“The scale and pace of both the challenge and opportunity presents a novel challenge for the sector and us as the regulator. We will continue to work with universities and colleges to help them reap the benefits of AI while avoiding the risks.”

The OfS said many institutions had already redesigned how they assessed students to reduce potential AI misuse, including greater use of in-person written exams or oral examinations known as vivas. Other examples include students critiquing or editing AI-generated output, or “process-based” assessments where students detail how they researched and produced their work.

A Department for Education spokesperson said: “We expect universities to take this issue seriously and we expect the OfS to both enforce the existing standards effectively, and work at pace to ensure its regulatory framework is explicit, strong and durable on the use of AI.”

The report by the OfS and Advance HE, a charity promoting university governance and teaching, interviewed more than 300 students and staff at 127 universities and colleges this year, to gauge AI policies and use in teaching and assessment.

One academic told the researchers: “AI has put academic integrity at serious risk … coursework is now overwhelmingly written in part, or exclusively, with the help of AI.”

Another university staff member said: “I think we’re realising that a number of our assessments may be unfit for purpose, and that pervasive use of AI may render our assessment of students close to impossible in some areas.”

The survey found that AI use was rife, with students saying their colleagues completed assessments using AI “sometimes in just a few minutes” and received similar grades to those who had completed an assessment without AI.

“Some students described their peers being unable to recall basic details about the assessment they had just submitted,” the report noted.

One student told the researchers: “I’ve had people admit, peer to peer, ‘I wrote this whole essay with ChatGPT’ … then they don’t get caught, they get a good grade probably, and then because it worked the first time, they do it on their next assessment.”

Academics also described receiving large numbers of submissions that looked the same, referenced the same literature and were written in the same style. Others said they believed the assessments used by their institution were not fit for purpose or did not accurately measure students’ knowledge and skills.

title: TEACHER VOICE: The future of personalized learning cannot be built on technology alone
summary:
By the time many of my high schoolers enter my algebra classroom, they already know what their school thinks they are bad at. They carry labels before they ever open a notebook: “remedial,” “unmotivated,” “low-performing.” Too often, personalized learning begins with those labels. The post TEACHER VOICE: The future of personalized learning cannot be built on technology alone appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
By the time many of my high schoolers enter my algebra classroom, they already know what their school thinks they are bad at. They carry labels before they ever open a notebook: “remedial,” “unmotivated,” “low-performing.”

Too often, personalized learning begins with those labels. We start with a low score or what we believe students cannot do — a missing skill or an academic gap — and then build instruction around fixing it.

I think we should start somewhere else: with what students care about, what they want to become and what already makes sense to them.

The starting point matters because personalized learning is supposed to do more than respond to academic gaps. Personalized learning is supposed to tailor instruction and learning experiences to support a student’s individual strengths, needs, interests, goals and pace.

But whether it fulfills that promise depends on the information we choose to prioritize. That prioritization matters even more as artificial intelligence becomes a bigger part of personalized learning.

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education.

AI gives teachers like me new ways to adapt instruction quickly. It can create practice problems, adjust reading levels, provide immediate feedback and generate materials based on student needs. But technology can only personalize the information we choose to give it.

That is why I believe a better approach to personalized learning with AI is giving it information to build learning from the student’s interests and goals. Otherwise, we risk using a new technology to make an old approach more entrenched instead of making learning more meaningful.

I saw what the difference could look like with a student I will call Kyle, who recently asked me, “If my phone can solve this in two seconds, why do I have to learn it?”

It was not a disrespectful question. It was an honest one. In an age of instant answers, more students are likely to wonder the same thing.

I could have responded with the usual answers: Because it is on the test, because you need the credits, because you will need this later.

Instead, I asked him what he cared about. Kyle started talking about cars, music and wanting to make money. That conversation gave us a way into the math.

Once I understood what mattered to him, I could use AI-supported personalized learning differently. I used it to generate examples connected to his interests, like comparing car loans and monthly payments and the long-term cost of financial decisions.

Through his interests, I was also able to give him work that allowed me to learn more about his ability than a worksheet or test score could have shown me. I saw how he reasoned when the context mattered to him. I saw where he got stuck, and I saw what made him willing to keep going. His confidence shifted because the math was no longer something being done to him. It became something connected to his future.

Generative AI can already support personalized learning in all the ways mentioned above. But if we are not careful, AI will sort students according to what they cannot do yet and call that innovation.

Related: OPINION: In the rush to adopt new AI technologies, let us not forget about the human touch

That is why I worry when personalized learning is defined only by academic level. Of course, I need to know where students are struggling. A math teacher like me cannot ignore gaps in understanding. But a student who struggles with equations may still be a sharp thinker when the math is connected to business, family responsibilities or sports.

In my classroom, I have learned that interest is not a distraction from rigor. It is often the entry point into it. AI helped me create relevant practice more quickly, but it did not create the reason for learning. That came from Kyle’s own goals and from the conversations we had in the classroom.

Academic data alone cannot tell me who a student is, how they think, what they value or what might make them willing to wrestle with something difficult. Starting with Kyle’s interests did not lower the mathematical expectations. It gave me a better way to help him reach them — with AI’s assistance.

That is the role that I think AI should play in personalized learning.

The starting point should be this: What do my students care about? What are they trying to become? What already makes sense to them?

Then AI can help me personalize the work and find ways to make it matter to them. In the process, my relationship with my students will deepen.

For students like Kyle, starting with who they are rather than what they are missing is what makes deeper learning possible. Knowing what matters to my students changes how I understand what they are capable of.

Al Rabanera teaches math at La Vista High School in Fullerton, California. He is a 2025-27 Teach Plus Leading Edge Educator Fellow.

title: States Make Progress on Outcomes-Based Higher Education
summary:
States Make Progress on Outcomes-Based Higher Education jessica.blake@… Tue, 11/10/2026 - 03:00 AM Higher ed systems across the country are improving when it comes to offering work-based learning, aligning with employers’ needs and providing career coaching, Strada’s third State Opportunity Index shows. Byline(s) Jessica Blake States Make Progress on Outcomes-Based Higher Education
jessica.blake@… Tue, 11/10/2026 - 03:00 AM

Higher ed systems across the country are improving when it comes to offering work-based learning, aligning with employers’ needs and providing career coaching, Strada’s third State Opportunity Index shows.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
In 2024, when the Strada Education Foundation first attempted to quantify and rate each state’s ability to ensure college students get a positive return on investment for their degree, none was deemed strong at providing work-based learning. Only about a quarter of bachelor’s degree graduates had completed a paid internship, the inaugural survey found.

Three years later, at least four states are considered strong on work-based learning opportunities and 12 are nearly there; meanwhile, 43 percent of graduating seniors say they’ve completed a paid, immersive work-based learning experience. States and public university systems have also improved when it comes to providing quality career coaching, aligning with employers’ needs and collecting clear outcomes data, the new 2026 Strada State Opportunities Index shows.

Since the nonprofit group began publishing this benchmark tool, they’ve seen “incredible progress,” said Dave Clayton, Strada’s senior vice president of research.

“When you look at state data infrastructures, we have firmly moved from a focus on access and then completion into an outcomes era,” he said. “You just see states flooding into that space, building integrated data systems and other resources to understand education-to-employment outcomes.”

Each year, the report has measured states’ performance in five areas that are critical to providing a positive return on investment: affordability, clear outcomes data, employer alignment, quality career coaching and work-based learning. And in each of the five categories, as well as a number of subcategories, metrics are then used to rate each state. The lowest score is “foundational,” middle tiers include “developing” and “advanced,” and the highest score is “leading.”

Not all metrics covered in the report, which was produced using a combination of student surveys and aggregated government data, show as significant a margin of growth as work-based learning. For example, the percentage of graduates nationally with a positive return on investment after 10 years only increased by about two percentage points from 2024 to 2025, remaining stagnant at 70 percent in 2026.

Clayton acknowledged the American higher education system has a long way to go before it connects all students to economic opportunity and meets the nation’s workforce needs. Still, he said, the overall trend demonstrates that state systems are making tangible steps forward.

“Ultimately, no, this year’s progress is not enough … We want every individual who invests their hopes, dreams, time and resources into pursuing postsecondary education to be better off financially,” he said. But “we’re delighted that people are making progress and that it’s showing up in ways that can be measured.”

When Strada first measured work-based learning for four-year degree programs in 2024, the nation was labeled as developing. Now, 16 states are either labeled advanced or sit right on the cusp between developing and advanced, though no state has yet reached the top tier.

Similar patterns can be seen in the four other categories. In 2024 only nine states demonstrated a strong enough data infrastructure to be deemed leading in the “clear outcomes” category, and 12 were advanced. Now those numbers are 17 and 22, respectively. Looking at affordability, 24 states earned a “leading” designation for associate degrees in 2024 and none for bachelor’s degrees; this year 35 states were rated “leading” for affordable associate degrees and two for affordable bachelors’.

In the few instances where states have appeared to slide backward—for instance, the number of leading states for “clear outcomes” fell from 20 last year to 17 this year—Clayton noted that Strada has actually raised the bar.

“So it was not going backwards. It was just saying we need to have more,” he said.

Strada also added two new elements to the 2026 index, called “states to watch” and “pathways to progress,” which highlight states that have made significant progress and the strategies they’re using. In one “states to watch” section, Indiana is spotlighted for establishing a consultant team at Ivy Tech Community College that develops more work-based opportunities through immediate partnerships with employers. A “pathways to progress” section notes that a number of states have established stipends for student teachers or apprenticeship programs for nurses, paying students to complete practicums that historically have been unpaid.

Clayton hopes the new feature will allow states to learn from one another, leading to continued improvement across all five categories. Eventually, he added, it should improve the nationwide return on investment.

“The power of the State Opportunity Index is that it’s a framework within which employers and providers of postsecondary education can have a shared discussion, both to identify the strengths they currently have, as well as areas where they can grow,” he said.

title: Farewell to the electoral college? Democrats now control enough states to elevate the popular vote
summary: Eighteen states run by Democrats have already joined an interstate compact to award their Electoral College votes to whichever presidential candidate wins the national popular vote.
full_text:
The sudden blue tint to so many more statehouses opens the door to enough states joining 18 other Democratic-run states in a deal that would effectively neuter the Electoral College. It would remake the battle for the presidency into one for the most votes nationwide, rather than candidates concentrating on a half dozen or so swing states.

READ MORE: Critics of Electoral College push for popular vote compact

The states that have joined what is known as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact account for 222 Electoral College votes. Once the number of states involved hits the 270 needed to win the presidency, the arrangement would effectively require a candidate to win the national popular vote to get an Electoral College majority.

It's not clear that the strategy has support from all the newly elected lawmakers and governors in the key states, and it's almost certain to draw legal challenges from conservative groups. If it does go forward, it could land before the conservative-majority Supreme Court.

Yet the sweep of the Democratic wins for governor and in state legislatures has the plan's supporters optimistic. In Tuesday's elections, Democrats won full control in six states representing 71 Electoral College votes: Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Minnesota, with its 10 electoral votes, had joined the compact when it was previously under full Democratic control in 2023.

Some governors express support while others are noncommittal

"We can do away with it," Wisconsin's new Democratic Gov. David Crowley said of the Electoral College, now that he has a legislature in his party's hands for the first time in 16 years. "I am interested in having those conversations with the state Legislature."

Over the weekend, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a likely 2028 contender for the Democratic presidential nomination, said he would like his newly Democratic legislature to take steps toward making the Electoral College obsolete.

"I think that the national popular vote makes sense. My views on that have not changed," Shapiro said on a liberal podcast. "I'll work with lawmakers to figure out what the right mechanism is for moving forward on that."

If Pennsylvania and Wisconsin supported the compact, reaching the 270 threshold would require Michigan and either Arizona or Nevada to join. On Tuesday, the office of Michigan's new Democratic governor, Jocelyn Benson, said it would not comment on the matter.

Not every Democratic governor is embracing the push yet. In a television interview on Monday, Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs declined to say whether she favored her state joining the compact. She said she's focused on other issues, like the cost of living.

Nevada's previous experience with the issue also is a cautionary tale for supporters.

WATCH: Can the Electoral College system be changed?

In 2019, then-Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak vetoed a measure that would have committed Nevada to joining the compact after it was passed by Democratic majorities in both houses of the Legislature. Sisolak said at the time that the popular vote idea would diminish the influence of smaller-population states like Nevada in national elections.

Democrats passed another measure to join the compact in 2023, but couldn't figure out a way around the state's then-Republican governor. Tai Sims, a spokesman for Nevada's incoming Democratic governor, Aaron Ford, said in a Tuesday statement, "There will be a time to talk about presidential elections, but right now Ford's focus is lowering costs for working families."

Republicans will use their diminished power to push back.

"Our Constitution gives states a voice in choosing the president for a reason," Tyler August, the Republican leader in the Wisconsin Assembly, said in a statement Tuesday. "This would undermine that balance and disenfranchise Wisconsin voters by letting results in other states override their choice."

Two presidents 16 years apart lost the popular vote

The idea of shifting to a national popular vote gained traction among Democrats after Republican George W. Bush won the 2000 presidential election by inching ahead of Democrat Al Gore in the Electoral College even while losing the popular vote. It became turbocharged after Republicans again won the White House that way in 2016 with Donald Trump's victory over Democrat Hillary Clinton.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Under the National Popular Vote plan, the candidate who wins the popular vote nationwide would receive the Electoral College votes from the states that have joined the compact.

There's nothing inherently partisan about the idea, said Patrick Rosenstiel, a Republican strategist in Minnesota who is a senior consultant to the popular vote movement. Occasionally GOP-majority legislative chambers, including the Oklahoma Senate, have passed proposals to join the compact, but the bills haven't gone further.

He said his own presidential vote is essentially meaningless because Minnesota has reliably voted Democratic in presidential elections for decades, leaving him with no say in the outcome and steering the vast majority of the candidates' attention elsewhere.

"I don't believe I've ever been relevant in the outcome of a presidential election," he said. "National popular vote forces campaigns to focus on every persuadable voter in every precinct across the nation."

Rosenstiel said the national popular vote campaign has been revving up to push the issue when the newly Democratic state legislatures convene at the start of the year. He said the organization has already lined up legislative sponsors.

The compact could create constitutional concerns

Republicans no longer have the power to stop the change in the Democratic-controlled states, but some conservative groups are prepared for a fight. The change "disenfranchises voters in member states if enacted, violates the United States Constitution, and undermines America's Founders' intent," wrote analysts for the America First Policy Institute, a pro-Trump think tank, in September.

There also is no guarantee the proposals will pass. Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor who is skeptical of the idea, said some might have second thoughts now that it's gone from a symbolic protest vote to a real possibility. He said there will be constitutional concerns, as well, that will likely lead to legal challenges.

The Constitution lets states run elections, and the Supreme Court in a case stemming from electors who sought to find a substitute for Trump in 2016 has ruled that states can require electors to vote for the presidential candidate they're pledged to.

Muller flagged potential legal hurdles to the popular vote plan. States have the power to run their elections but not set rules that will determine the outcome in other states' contests. Additionally, each state ballot is different, and some would potentially have third-party candidates who wouldn't appear elsewhere, leading to the dilution of a vote for a Democrat or Republican in one state compared to another.

That could violate the 14th Amendment's requirement that everyone have "equal protection of the laws." The U.S. Supreme Court also might decide that states can't join a compact to change one of their core constitutional duties, unless they get congressional approval.

"I think the Supreme Court will be interested," Muller said.

Bauer reported from Madison, Wis. Associated Press writers Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pa., Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Jessica Hill in Las Vegas and Mikella Schuettler in Phoenix contributed to this report.

title: Alberta's United Conservative Party faces backlash for pledge that limits riding presidents' independence talk
summary: Some senior party organizers refuse to sign a new NDA stating they'll "abide by" the referendum result.
full_text:
The UCP is facing pushback from some of its top organizers for demanding all riding presidents sign a non-disclosure agreement that declares they “recognize, respect and will abide by” results of the separation referendum.

This new demand comes weeks after three-quarters of Albertans voted to keep the province in Canada rather than pursue independence — and Premier Danielle Smith urged UCP members to accept the outcome and move on, or leave for another party.

Party brass recently made candidates for upcoming provincial board elections sign a declaration that they will abide by the referendum decision. Now it’s extending that condition to all 87 current presidents of UCP constituency associations.

“I understand and acknowledge that my public statements and actions as a CA president will have a direct impact on the reputation of the CA and the association,” says the combination NDA and code of conduct sent by party executive director Dustin van Vugt, and obtained by CBC News.

“Accordingly, I wish to clearly state that I recognize, respect, and will abide by the majority decision made by Albertans on Question #10 of the 26/10/19 referendum.”

In an email to riding presidents, van Vugt requested they all sign and return the pledge by this Friday.

But multiple riding presidents are reluctant or unwilling to sign the document, and are calling it an unfair way to stifle their speech.

“It’s not wise to be trying to suppress when we should be trying to unify,” said Darrell Komick, president of the United Conservative association for Calgary-Lougheed.

“That’s the sort of thing that will stop people from volunteering.”

Komick has led one of the party’s most outspoken local groups, having hosted past forums that questioned Alberta’s place within Canada and the safety of COVID vaccines. He also ran unsuccessfully for party president last fall, promising a greater embrace of the pro-independence position.

“As the party of free speech, we should understand that that comes with risks as a party, but it also comes with rewards,” Komick told CBC News.

The riding presidents opposed to the party’s new NDA span both sides of the referendum question that has divided party members. One said that at least 15 presidents are signing their own letter to the party explaining that they refuse to endorse the NDA.

“It appears a jam-down by certain people at the upper reaches of the party to squash any public embarrassment or public conflict about independence, and it’s just wrong,” said one president, who did not want to use their name for fear of retribution.

This president, who opposes Alberta independence, questioned why only one divisive issue is highlighted in this non-disclosure form.

“We have back and forth about friggin’ abortion,” said the constituency president. “Why are we singling out this one issue? It’s just ridiculous.”

The source said this agreement appears at odds with a section of the party’s existing code of conduct, which says that constituency association board members shall “not be reprimanded or disciplined by the party... or CA board for exercising their freedom of expression unless such expression constitutes an offence under the Criminal Code of Canada.”

United Conservative officials did not reply to CBC News’ questions before deadline.

Even though Smith had repeatedly declared support for keeping Alberta within Canada, detractors accused her of being too supportive of the separatists within UCP ranks, and making it easier to get the independence question onto the ballot.

But in the days after October’s resounding pro-unity decision, Smith declared the United Conservatives are clearly pro-unity as a party, and that no candidates or MLAs would be allowed to support independence.

“It also means we expect every member of our provincial board and members of constituency association boards across the province to uphold the position of our party on this issue,” the premier said in a video statement to party members last month.

While it was vastly unpopular among most segments of Albertans, about half of UCP supporters supported the pro-independence option in the referendum, according to polling before the vote.

The premier has since faced pockets of resistance from her UCP base, including separatist activists frustrated she took sides in the referendum.

Five riding associations have endorsed subjecting Smith to a leadership review, although most other party constituency groups passed motions opposing a review, meaning that her place in the party is under no immediate threat.

Some pro-independence activists are running for places on the UCP provincial board at the party convention in Calgary later this month. They endorsed the declaration that they’d abide by the unity referendum’s results, but said they’d continue to freely advocate for more “sovereignty” for Alberta within Canada in the short term.

While non-disclosure agreements and codes of conduct are not unusual for not-for-profit organizations, it’s odd to see a policy declaration tucked inside it, one governance expert told CBC News.

“When you're involved in a governing body, you can't pre-commit your political stance,” said Nolan Crouse, instructor and lead expert with the board development program at MacEwan University in Edmonton.

“When I walk into a meeting, I'm supposed to be open-minded. But the verbiage here looks like that the provincial association is pre-committing you to a political stance or [to] ‘abide by’ something, right?”

Crouse, the former mayor of St. Albert, said he’s surprised the form passed “the acid test” among UCP’s leadership and top governance officials.

Frustration over Smith's new push to steer the UCP away from separatism emerged this week at an Edmonton forum for party board candidates.

"Now I'm a little confused when our leader tells us if you're not a federalist, you do not belong in this party, and then you're going to come to me and ask for my money and help to door-knock?" said Wade Collinge, a Sylvan Lake resident wearing a separatist group's T-shirt.

"Whose party is this? Is this Danielle's party or is it the members party?"

Rob Smith, the provincial UCP president, interrupted from the front of the room to defend the premier.

"She's not asking you to be a federalist," he said. "She's not asking anyone to be a federalist. She's saying: respect the result of 75 per cent of Albertans."

The UCP president added that not a single dollar of party money went toward advocating on either side of the unity referendum, though the party did campaign on the other nine questions.

title: Global PBSA leaders outline China’s new student-centric era
summary:
The global international student housing and education sectors stand at a critical inflection point, marked by a structural shift from supply shortages to an oversupplied market in key university hubs.

The post Global PBSA leaders outline China’s new student-centric era appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
At the Funliving Global Partner Conference and Tomato Education International’s 10th Anniversary Conference held on October 16, industry leaders, accommodation operators, and study-abroad partners gathered to launch a unified operational roadmap for the evolving study-abroad ecosystem.

Despite macro-level economic rebalancing, international student demand remains strong – especially in popular student cities including London, Manchester, Hong Kong, and Singapore.

Key findings presented by Funliving’s COO Jeffery Yang at the summit revealed that student inquiries rose 25% year-on-year, with confirmed accommodation bookings increasing by 19%.

Studio and one-bedroom share bookings grew by 3.2%, accompanied by an average rent increase of 11% across eight major international markets. Secondary destinations such as Manchester and Edinburgh recorded the fastest growth.

Data from the panellists from organisations including Funliving Digital, British Council and EIC further reaffirmed these market fundamentals. Total Chinese study demand, including overseas study, domestic TNE programs, and regional hubs is once again nearing its 2019 peak, indicating market diversification rather than overall contraction.

In-person UK enrolment stands at over 140,000 Chinese students, with direct undergraduate applications from mainland China reaching 38,000, and 61% securing offers from QS Top 100 universities.

Meanwile, the average timeline from initial student contact to confirmed housing booking quadrupled from 11 days to over 44 days, requiring longer, highly responsive follow-up workflows.

Social media feeds and verified peer reviews have replaced traditional search routes as primary discovery channels. To engage students earlier in their research phase, operators and partners are co-creating city-level content and co-branded storytelling that showcase authentic local living, safety, and neighbourhood culture alongside accommodation details.

Summer Zhao, digital marketing director at Funliving, highlighted that in China, as traffic becomes increasingly expensive, the only thing that truly stays on social media is content.

Wu Xinping from the British Council Beijing noted that the one-year UK Master’s degree originated during the British Industrial Revolution to rapidly cultivate applied talents. Featuring high course density and heavy academic intensity, it is far from the “low-quality degree” rumoured in some Chinese markets.

When talking about what new generation of students truly expect, delegates warned operators against the “homogeneous product trap”: blindly investing in premium amenities such as cinemas and rooftop lounges that students rarely use.

Students are a sophisticated and valued audience and when travelling to the UK it is increasingly important we offer more than just a bed to sleep in

Paul Watson, Now Student Living

Instead, the new generation of international students prioritises practical and full-cycle support including efficient layouts with ample storage, in-unit or accessible laundry facilities, and rransparent, verified room details and 24/7 service support throughout the entire stay cycle.

Paul Watson, managing director at Now Student Living stated: “Students are a sophisticated and valued audience and when travelling to the UK it is increasingly important we offer more than just a bed to sleep in. We are proud to offer safety and security alongside a community for students to feel part of and so their families feel confident they are being looked after”.

A core milestone of the summit was establishing a clear strategic distinction between ordinary channels and long-term partners. While ordinary channels operate with a narrow focus on short-term booking volumes and commission fees, partners focus on mutual brand amplification and aligned long-term goals.

In addition, partners supply vital local market intelligence, regional recruitment insight, and on-ground student service support. Rather than limiting their involvement strictly to initial booking transactions, strategic partners serve as an extended support team providing 24/7 service coordination across the entire student stay cycle.

Central to this partnership model is transparent data sharing and technical integration. Operators and partners agreed to move beyond sharing final booking numbers by opening real-time visibility across the entire conversion funnel, including inquiry rates and student feedback.

Crucially, true partners support cross-region brand growth while avoiding price competition that cannibalises the same student source markets. As a result, summit delegates agreed to move away from destructive commission price wars and “race-to-the-bottom” cashback schemes, transitioning toward multi-dimensional evaluation systems that assess partners on lead generation, brand exposure, inquiry volume, and overall service quality.

Panels featuring universities, payment providers, and accommodation operators reached strong consensus that post-offer and arrival support represents the next major value driver for student satisfaction.

title: AIEC 2026: Australia rethinks its international education promise
summary:
At its 40th conference in Sydney, the Australian sector confronted visa uncertainty, global competition and the need to make a more credible case to students and the public.

The post AIEC 2026: Australia rethinks its international education promise appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
More than 1,750 delegates gathered at Sydney’s International Convention Centre from October 27-30 for the 40th Australian International Education Conference (AIEC), a milestone that proved less a victory lap than a reckoning.

Under the banner “Future Thinking”, AIEC 2026 faced a question: how can Australia remain a trusted study destination as student mobility, migration policy and public confidence continue to shift?

Australia arrived at the conference on uncertain ground. Preliminary government data showed overseas higher education commencements were down 4.9% year on year in early 2026.

The government has retained a national planning level of 295,000 new overseas commencements for 2027, even as changes to student dependants, onshore pathways and course transfers reshape the conditions under which Australian institutions recruit and support students.

Assistant minister Julian Hill brought visa certainty to the center of that discussion. He acknowledged that refusal rates were affecting key markets and deterring the students Australia most wants to attract.

No decisions have been made but a Home Affairs consultation is considering changes to Genuine Student assessments and financial-capacity evidence, including options for students to hold relevant funds in an Australian bank account before lodging a visa application.

“Even if this means raising the financial standards and a smaller pool of prospective students, I want grant rates to improve and greater certainty for everyone,” Hill said.

Prospective students are already responding to the wider uncertainty. IDP research released during AIEC found Australia’s first-choice share had slipped to 24%, following an almost one-quarter fall in six months, while more than four in five students surveyed were comparing multiple destinations.

Cost, visa prospects, policy stability and post-study options are now central to that comparison. At a student roundtable hosted by The PIE News, participants described what those choices look like in lived rather than statistical terms.

They spoke of misleading advice from migration agents before arrival, support that can be difficult to access once enrolled, and employment criteria that can favor domestic applicants or graduates.

Several linked financial pressure and uncertainty to the mental wellbeing of students and their families.

Students also resisted being framed solely as temporary visitors or an economic category. They spoke about checking on peers, building communities and contributing to the country around them, asking to be recognised as part of local life.

That combination of security, belonging and future prospects ran through AIEC’s discussion of employability.

“There is a difference between employability and employment,” Austrade South Asia trade and investment commissioner Vik Singh said. “Employment is not the answer. Employability is the answer.”

For students and families, rankings may open a door, but career pathways determine whether the investment makes sense. Speakers called for internships, work-integrated learning, employer engagement and career guidance to be embedded from the beginning of a student’s journey.

India offered a clear test of that proposition. With international providers opening or planning campuses in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad, speakers said an international credential would need to be matched by local career outcomes, mobility options and trusted partnerships.

Panelists said the still-young model has few at-scale precedents and will compete not only with other overseas providers but with local universities that have established employer links and graduate networks.

“India doesn’t want a scattering of MoUs that hang on the wall,” Singh said. “It’s deeper partnerships that deliver.”

What would it look like if hope and trust were the watchwords as we built the future of education for international and domestic students? That would be a real delineator, I think

Julia Gillard, former Prime Minister of Australia

Transnational education (TNE) featured prominently throughout the conference, but was not presented as an escape route from a more difficult onshore market.

At a policy session, Universities Australia CEO Luke Sheehy cautioned against assuming that “the future is offshore”, while education minister Jason Clare made the case for delivery closer to students.

“Not everyone can come here to study. Not everyone can afford it. But we can come to them,” Clare said.

The global dialogue showed that Australia is far from alone in reassessing its model.

Canada is reducing volume while prioritising sustainability and graduate talent, New Zealand is pursuing growth within quality safeguards, and US institutions are being urged to adapt to a more multipolar higher education landscape.

“Business as usual is over,” said Michigan State University’s John Hudzik, who argued that “internationalisation is not just about teaching and learning. It’s also about research collaboration.”

That broader definition was echoed by delegates who urged Australia to connect international education more closely with research partnerships across the Indo-Pacific.

The question of public legitimacy also returned repeatedly. IEAA chief executive Phil Honeywood described a “conundrum of profit motive versus the public good,” arguing that the sector needed to show it was about more than fee income and migration settings.

In video interviews with The PIE, delegates called for a stronger social case for international students, more innovative employability support and recruitment strategies that look beyond the next intake.

They also cautioned that evidence alone will not shift public attitudes. The sector needs to explain, in local and human terms, what students bring to communities and why their experiences matter.

That attention to listening was evident beyond the main sessions. At the IEAA Excellence Awards, miXabroad won for a global benchmark that enables institutions to compare student experience and impact across learning-abroad programs, cohorts and countries.

Separately, six Australian providers backed a new benchmark intended to put student feedback at the center of education-agent evaluation.

At the close of the conference, attention turned to the Gold Coast, which will host AIEC 2027 from November 9 to 12 under the theme “New Generation, New World”.

IDP Education chief executive Tennealle O’Shannessy said the conference had shown that the sector must continue to collaborate as technology evolves and policy settings fluctuate.

“The priorities we’ve aligned on in Sydney now need to be carried forward,” Honeywood said. “As we head to the Gold Coast in 2027, we’re committed to ensuring international education remains a valued and trusted part of Australia’s future.”

Former Australian Prime Minister Julia Gillard gave that challenge a wider political and educational frame in her closing keynote.

She urged universities to share authority with students and involve them meaningfully in shaping the future of education, particularly in a more cynical and distrustful public environment.

On the increasingly fraught debate around international students, Gillard said: “I think the only way of working through it is with the authenticity of local stories and community engagement.”

Her final question captured the task that will follow the sector to the Gold Coast and beyond: “What would it look like if hope and trust were the watchwords as we built the future of education for international and domestic students? That would be a real delineator, I think.”

title: Natalie Field, IDP
summary:
This week, The PIE sat down with Natalie Field, chief experience officer – student placement at IDP. We spoke about building confidence into the student journey, the unglamorous foundations behind transformation and why international education should help students create work as well as find it.

The post Natalie Field, IDP appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Describe yourself in three words or phrases.

A builder at heart. Someone who sees possibility in people and in the future. Tenacious when something matters.

What do you like most about your job?

What I love most is the chance to make a difference at a really important moment in someone’s life. Choosing where and what to study can shape a student’s future and helping them make that choice with confidence, across so many countries and cultures, is a huge privilege. I also love the scope and range of my role. On any given day I’m thinking about customer experience, people, technology, policy and economics. The most interesting problems and opportunities are often found in the connections between these areas.

Describe a project or initiative you’re currently working on that excites you.

I’m working on how we reimagine the student journey so that every interaction leaves a student better informed and more confident in their choice. Technology and AI can play a huge role in that, but what excites me most is what we can unlock on the human side: giving our people more time, better insight and the ability to bring real judgement and care to the moments that matter. When a student has confidence in their decision, everyone benefits, including the institution they choose.

What’s a piece of work you’re proud of, and what did it teach you?

Some of the work I’m proudest of is work nobody would ever see. Throughout my career, I’ve worked on building data foundations that have enabled much bigger changes later. It was painstaking at times, and certainly wasn’t the glamorous part of transformation, but it reinforced for me that great things usually sit on top of really good plumbing. You need people who can see the future you’re trying to create and still have the tenacity to do the hard, detailed work required to get there. My experience has taught me to value both: ambition about what’s possible and the discipline to make it real.

What’s a small daily habit that helps you in your work?

I journal at the end of each day: what I’m grateful for, the moments of joy worth celebrating, anything I need to forgive, in myself or others, and any loose ends I need to pick up the next day.

This practice helps me finish the day with intention and gives me a fighting chance of a good night’s sleep!

What’s one change you’d like to see in your sector over the next few years?

I’d love to see international education become known not just for helping students find meaningful work, but for helping them create it. Universities already do great things in entrepreneurship and innovation, and I think we can go much further: making business building, problem solving and economic contribution part of the student experience from the beginning. International students bring extraordinary ambition, global networks and perspectives that cross borders. If we help turn more of that into businesses, ideas and innovation, the value to students, institutions and the countries that welcome them multiplies.

I’ve always believed we should try to create more than we consume, and I’d love to see international education become one of the places where that really comes to life.

What idea, book, podcast or conversation has stayed with you recently?

A conversation with my son about politics, systems thinking and how we create change. We were talking about how easy it is to feel overwhelmed when a problem is enormous and every issue seems connected to 10 others.

We spoke about how complexity can sometimes become an excuse for doing nothing. His perspective was refreshing : take action, learn from it, and then do the next thing. It was such a good reminder that you rarely need to know the whole route before you start.

It’s a simple thought, but one that applies to so many parts of our personal and professional lives.

What’s one piece of advice you’d give to someone starting out in this field?

I’m relatively new to the industry myself, so my advice probably applies regardless of industry: stay curious and keep learning for life. The tools and technologies in our sector will keep changing and maturing (and yes including AI!), but some capabilities only become more valuable: asking good questions, thinking critically, breaking a messy problem into parts you can solve, and learning from people who see the world differently.

And don’t be afraid to get things wrong. Be disciplined in your thinking, but take action. If you make a mistake, own it, learn from it and keep going. A career is long. Curiosity and the willingness to keep learning will take you further than having all the answers.

title: ASEAN-UK higher education partnerships must reflect local priorities
summary:
ASEAN and UK higher education leaders have called for more locally driven partnerships, backed by clear regulation and funding, as universities look to deepen collaboration on skills, research and AI.

The post ASEAN-UK higher education partnerships must reflect local priorities appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Speaking at a panel during the British Council-led ASEAN-UK Education Week in Manila, speakers stressed that transnational education (TNE) and research partnerships must be shaped around the needs of local institutions and economies, rather than simply exporting UK models overseas.

Michelle Aguilar-Ong, commissioner of the Philippines’ Commission on Higher Education (CHED), said the Philippines was preparing to launch a national strategy for transnational higher education, identifying digital transformation, renewable energy and the blue economy as priority areas for international cooperation.

She also highlighted the pace of change in the global skills landscape, warning that “by 2030, 39% of the skills today won’t be relevant anymore”.

Speakers also said partnerships would need to move beyond high-level discussions and translate into practical collaboration between institutions.

Kostantino Kontis, chair of the UUKi Asia Network and dean for global engagement in China and East Asia, at the University of Glasgow, said even modest amounts of seed funding could help bring academics together and establish the foundations for longer-term partnerships.

Universities should “co-design programs that the partner identifies as valuable”, he said, rather than simply transplanting existing UK models into local contexts.

Daley Middleton, head of trade at the UK’s Department for Education, advocated for the UK’s “extensive” TNE experience, “world-class quality” as reasons why British universities would make good partners.

But he pointed out that ASEAN countries have other options open to them. “As fabulous as we are [in the UK], ASEAN does not necessarily need to choose one partner, and we obviously encourage everyone to advocate for their own needs,” he said.

Middleton highlighted the scale of existing engagement, with more than 39,000 students from Southeast Asia studying at UK higher education institutions in the last academic year. More than 96,000 students across the region were also involved in UK TNE programs.

“These are not just impressive figures,” he said. “They represent decades of institutional partnerships, research collaborations and people-to-people connections.”

These are not just impressive figures. They represent decades of institutional partnerships, research collaborations and people-to-people connections

Daley Middleton, UK Department for Education

The future of international education would be about more than student mobility alone, Middleton added, pointing to the growing importance of TNE, joint degrees and research partnerships.

Meanwhile, the UK’s ambassador to ASEAN, Helen Fazey, reiterated the UK’s commitment to ASEAN and its institutions, pointing to the strength of the relationship and the importance attached to engagement with the region.

Universities including Reading, Leeds, Liverpool, Newcastle, Goldsmiths and Liverpool Hope are already working with local partners to develop joint programs.

And addressing the conference via video link, the UK’s international education champion Sir Steve Smith said the UK viewed ASEAN as a long-term partner in education, research and skills, adding that successful TNE partnerships should strengthen both institutions involved.

Students should receive excellent teaching, appropriate support and clear information about their qualifications, he said.

title: Beyond the Grade: Turning Feedback Into Teaching With the IDE CARES Model

The post Beyond the Grade: Turning Feedback Into Teaching With the IDE CARES Model appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
A student once told me that after reading my feedback, she turned to her husband and said, “Ide cares.” That comment stayed with me.

It was kind, of course, but it also captured something I had been trying to do in my courses for years: hold students to meaningful academic and professional standards while making sure they understood that my feedback was meant to help them grow, not simply explain why they lost points.

That moment eventually led me to name the feedback approach I had already been using: the IDE CARES Feedback Model. The model is designed for faculty who want feedback that goes beyond justifying a grade. It helps students understand what they did well, where they need to improve, why the standard matters, and how to carry the feedback into their next submission.

I developed the model in health administration courses, but the structure can work in many settings, especially online, hybrid, writing-intensive, or accelerated courses where written feedback may be the main one-on-one teaching students receive.

Why Feedback Needs More Structure

Many of us were taught some version of the “feedback sandwich”: begin with something positive, address what needs improvement, and close with encouragement. That structure can be helpful, but on its own, it is not always enough.

Students may appreciate the positive tone but still leave unsure what to revise. They may see a rubric score but not understand how their work missed the standard. They may read “APA needs work” or “analysis needs more depth” and not know what those comments actually require them to do next.

Recent feedback research points to a practical reality many faculty already see: feedback only helps when students understand it and know what to do next. Williams (2024) describes effective feedback as a contributor to student motivation, learning, and performance, while also noting that feedback practices can be difficult to deliver well. Dawson et al. (2024) focus on what students actually do with feedback, including how they seek it, make sense of it, use it, and manage their response to it. For instructors, the takeaway is straightforward: feedback should be clear, usable, and connected to the next attempt. That is where IDE CARES comes in.

I: Identify Strengths and Growth Areas

Start by naming what the student did well and where growth is needed. This should be specific, not generic.

Instead of writing, “Good job,” try:

“You selected a relevant topic and clearly understand why this issue matters in practice. The next step is to strengthen the paper by connecting your major claims to scholarly or authoritative sources.”

This opening does two things. It shows the student that you actually read the work, and it frames correction as part of growth rather than punishment.

D: Direct Students Back to the Rubric and Assignment Directions

Students can take grading personally when they cannot see how the comments connect to the assignment expectations. Directing students back to the rubric helps them see that the feedback is tied to criteria, not instructor preference.

For example:

“The rubric requires evidence-supported analysis. Right now, the paper includes a reference page, but the body paragraphs do not include in-text citations showing where source information was used.”

That type of comment is much more useful than “Needs citations.” It tells the student what standard was missed and where to look.

E: Explain Why the Standard Matters

Students are more likely to use feedback when they understand why the issue matters beyond the assignment.

In my courses, I often explain that APA, citation use, professional tone, and evidence-based reasoning are not just academic requirements. They are workplace skills. Future professionals need to document decisions, support recommendations, and communicate clearly with supervisors, colleagues, patients, clients, or community partners.

A feedback comment might say:

“In-text citations are important because they allow the reader to verify the evidence behind your claims. In professional settings, unsupported recommendations can weaken credibility and decision-making.”

This helps students understand that the standard is not just my preference. It is part of the professional skill set they are building.

C: Clarify the Correction Needed

Vague feedback rarely leads to strong revision. Students need to know what to do.

Instead of writing, “Expand this section,” try:

“To strengthen this section, add one current scholarly or authoritative source, explain how it supports your point, and connect the evidence back to the assignment question.”

Instead of “Improve discussion replies,” try:

“In your next reply, directly reference one point your peer made, add a new idea or example, and ask a question that moves the discussion forward.”

Clarifying the correction turns feedback into a next step.

A: Apply Feedback Through Revision or Resubmission Opportunities

This is one of the most important parts of the model. Feedback should not always be the endpoint of learning.

When course policy allows, I invite students to revise or resubmit lower-scoring assignments after reviewing my feedback. I frame this as an opportunity, not a requirement and not a punishment. The message is simple: detailed feedback is most valuable when students are allowed to use it.

A practical resubmission note might read:

“You are welcome to revise and resubmit this assignment after reviewing the feedback. Focus first on adding in-text citations to each major body paragraph, strengthening the analysis section, and correcting the reference page format.”

Faculty should be clear about deadlines, eligibility, and grading limits. But when possible, revision gives students a chance to demonstrate learning rather than simply move on with a low score.

R: Reinforce Confidence While Maintaining Standards

Supportive feedback should not erase expectations. Students need encouragement, but they also need to know the standard still matters.

For example:

“You have a strong topic and a clear interest in this issue. To reach the next level, the paper needs stronger source integration and closer alignment with the assignment criteria.”

This type of feedback communicates belief in the student while preserving rigor. It avoids two extremes: harsh comments that discourage students and overly soft comments that do not lead to improvement.

E: Encourage Questions and Support-Seeking

Students may not know how to interpret feedback on their own. Invite them into the process.

A simple sentence can help:

“Please reach out if you would like help applying this feedback before your next submission.”

You can also direct students to writing centers, library support, APA resources, office hours, sample papers, recorded walkthroughs, or course announcements. In online courses especially, students may need repeated reminders that asking for clarification is part of learning.

S: Support Continued Professional Growth

Close by connecting the feedback to who the student is becoming.

In a healthcare course, I might write:

“As you continue preparing for healthcare leadership roles, the ability to support recommendations with credible evidence will strengthen your professional communication and decision-making.”

In another discipline, the wording may change, but the purpose is the same. Students should understand that writing, reasoning, revision, evidence use, and professional communication are not just classroom tasks. They are transferable skills.

Using IDE CARES in Discussions and Assignments

For written assignments, I often begin with a short overall comment, then move criterion by criterion through the rubric. Under each criterion, I identify what worked, explain what limited the score, and give a clear action step. I usually end with two or three priorities for revision or the next assignment.

For discussions, I use the same model in a shorter form. I might acknowledge a student’s relevant point, direct them back to the expectation for evidence or peer engagement, clarify what a stronger reply would include, and encourage them to ask a question or bring in a specific example next time.

This approach also works well for class-wide feedback. If several students miss the same expectation, I post an announcement or short walkthrough before the next assignment. That saves time and helps students see common patterns.

Making Feedback Manageable

Detailed feedback takes time, but it can be made more sustainable. I recommend creating a feedback bank organized by common rubric areas: content, analysis, source use, APA, organization, discussion engagement, and professionalism. Then personalize each comment with at least one detail from the student’s actual submission.

A “next steps” section also helps. Students do not always need ten things to fix at once. They need to know which two or three changes matter most.

The goal is not to write more feedback for the sake of writing more. The goal is to write feedback students can actually use.

Feedback is Teaching

Feedback should not merely explain a grade after learning is over. It should help students keep learning.

The IDE CARES model gives faculty a practical way to make feedback specific, compassionate, rigorous, and actionable. It reminds students that we see their effort, that standards matter, and that improvement is possible.

When feedback is done well, students do not just learn what they got wrong. They learn how to revise, how to think more deeply, how to communicate more professionally, and how to carry those skills into the next assignment and beyond.

That is the kind of feedback students remember. More importantly, it is the kind they can use.

Dr. Dawn Ide is a healthcare administration educator and curriculum developer with more than 15 years of experience teaching across face-to-face, hybrid, and online postsecondary settings. Her work focuses on healthcare administration education, online learning, assessment design, academic integrity, and workforce preparation.

The post The AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio: Redesigning Assignments for an AI-Augmented Classroom appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
We are at a pivotal moment in education. The rise of generative AI has forced a widespread re-evaluation of how we assess student learning. For decades, the take-home essay, the research paper, and the report have been mainstays of assessment—primarily “product-based” assignments where the final artifact is the main object of evaluation.

AI directly challenges this model by making the production of polished text, code, or images trivial. The question facing college and university faculty is not whether to address this reality, but how to respond with intention. The AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio is my attempt to provide a practical, structured answer—one grounded in a framework that centers the uniquely human journey of learning.

The honest origin of this resource is simpler than any theoretical framework. Faculty kept coming to me with the same question: “How do I get my students to stop using AI?” I understood the frustration behind it. But I also knew that policing students into compliance was not a pedagogy—it was a surveillance strategy. And contestability—the exhausting back-and-forth of trying to prove whether a student used AI—was consuming faculty energy that belonged in the classroom. So instead of asking how we stop students from using AI, I started asking a different question: what would we have to design so that the learning itself could not be outsourced? That reframe became the Studio. I built it as a free, openly licensed OER resource because I did not want cost or access to be the barrier between a faculty member and a better approach. Every instructor deserves a practical starting point, not just a policy to enforce.

What the Studio Is

The AI-Resistant Pedagogy Studio: An Interactive Toolkit for Assignment Redesign is a living document—hosted at https://ynaqbxzy.manus.space/ and regularly updated with current research and vetted best practices—that I developed and published in 2025 (Evans, 2026). It is organized into eight sections: Overview, In the News, Tool Landscape, Framework, Strategies, Best Practices, Case Studies, and a hands-on interactive Toolkit.

Its core premise: as AI tools become more prevalent, our role as educators shifts. We are not just imparting knowledge—we are fostering human capacities that resist automation. The strength of our communities—our classrooms, our departments, our institutions—is our greatest asset in this work.

Since its release, the Studio has been adopted as a faculty development resource at institutions across the country. These include Clemson University, South Dakota University, Washington University, Hood College, the University of Houston-Downtown, Loyola-Notre Dame, and Roman University—each using the Studio to train faculty on redesigning assignments that are resilient to generative AI, shifting their professional development programs away from detection and toward intentional pedagogical design. The Studio has also reached beyond traditional higher education: it was featured on page 7 of the American Art Therapy Association (AATA) Undergraduate Art Therapy Educators Newsletter, where practitioners highlighted its value for deepening the human connections and critical thinking central to their field (AATA Newsletter, 2026). That the Studio has found traction in art therapy education, research universities, liberal arts colleges, and Hispanic-Serving Institutions alike speaks to something universal in the problem it addresses: faculty everywhere are asking the same question, and they need more than a policy in response.

From Product to Process: The Central Shift

The Studio is built around a necessary and accelerated shift toward process-based assessment. This approach emphasizes the uniquely human journey of learning: the research process, the collaborative dialogue, the critical self-reflection, and the iterative development of an idea. The focus moves from “what did you produce?” to “how did you learn, and what can you do with that knowledge?” (Evans, 2026).

When AI can produce a satisfactory first draft in seconds, the skills that become more valuable are those AI struggles with: critical evaluation of AI-generated content, creative synthesis of multiple sources, ethical reasoning, and personal reflection. Practically, process-based assessment means building systems that value:

Multi-stage assignments—proposals, annotated bibliographies, drafts, and final versions—that make the research process visible and gradable

Oral defenses or brief one-on-one conferences that verify individual understanding and ensure knowledge resides with the student, not the tool

AI critique tasks: having students analyze AI-generated output for flaws, biases, and weaknesses (Cornell University, n.d.)

Community-based and experiential projects grounded in local, real-world contexts where AI cannot physically participate

Three Core Strategies for AI-Resistant Design

The Studio organizes its assignment redesign framework around three strategies, each targeting something AI genuinely cannot replicate.

1. Collaborative Inquiry

Assignments requiring genuine, interdependent collaboration—where the process of interaction and shared knowledge construction is as important as the product. AI struggles with the nuanced, dynamic, and often messy process of real human interaction, negotiation, and shared ownership. Practical examples include jigsaw presentations, team-based learning structures, and structured peer review of drafts (Evans, 2026).

2. Authentic Engagment

Assignments that connect learning to real-world contexts, lived experiences, and tangible community needs. AI lacks lived experience, embodied knowledge, sensory perception, and the ability to navigate the unpredictable complexities of the real world. Oral history interviews, community-partner projects, and primary source fieldwork all require students to gather information no AI model can access (Evans, 2026).

3. Metacognitive Reflection

Assignments that require students to reflect on their own learning process, document their thinking, and critically evaluate their methods and tools. AI cannot engage in genuine self-reflection or authentic introspection about its own learning journey. Learning portfolios with reflection essays, process documentation projects, and AI usage and ethics reflections all center this uniquely human capacity (Evans, 2026).

The Equity Dimension

No discussion of AI-resistant pedagogy is complete without addressing equity. A reliance on technology can exacerbate the digital divide, disadvantaging students without reliable access to high-speed internet or modern devices. Furthermore, since many AI models are trained on biased data, their outputs can reinforce harmful stereotypes (Frontiers in Education, 2024; Shelton & Lanier, 2024).

The Studio addresses this directly: an equitable approach requires designing assessments that do not depend on premium AI tools and explicitly teaching students to identify and critique algorithmic bias. This means designing for the baseline—if a tool is not institutionally provided, it should not be required for the grade. It also means advocating for campus-wide licenses and providing dedicated in-class lab time so access does not determine academic success (Evans, 2026).

In my own work leading the Center for Teaching Excellence at Our Lady of the Lake University, an HSI institution, this equity lens is not optional—it is foundational. The Studio’s framework was built with under-resourced students and under-supported faculty explicitly in mind.

Redefining Academic Integrity

The focus of academic integrity is moving beyond a narrow definition of plagiarism toward a broader concept of ethical and transparent use of tools. Rather than simply banning AI, institutions are developing policies that require students to acknowledge and document their use of AI—shifting the conversation from “did you cheat?” to “how did you use this tool responsibly?” This requires a culture of honesty built on proactive pedagogy rather than reactive detection (Packback, 2025; Sabourin Laflamme & Bruneault, 2025).

Practically, this means building in AI disclosure statements, requiring prompt histories alongside final submissions, and explaining the pedagogical rationale behind assignments so students understand what skills they are developing—and why those skills matter in a world with AI.

Faculty Development as the Engine of Change

Educators cannot be expected to navigate this new landscape alone. There is an urgent need for intentional, institutionally supported faculty development—training that goes beyond demonstrating how to use a new tool and focuses instead on pedagogical redesign and fair assessment strategy (Kolomitro & Schultz, 2024; Educause, 2024).

This is the work I do. Through conference presentations at venues including the NISOD Virtual Conference, the Northeast OER Summit, the Rutgers Online Learning Conference, the Innovative Teaching & Learning Conference, and the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board’s Digital Learning Summit, I have brought the Studio’s framework to faculty across disciplines and institution types. Additional engagements have included Educause, the University of Rhode Island, and the University of Tennessee.

When I present the Studio, I organize sessions around a single provocation: your current assignments may be measuring AI fluency, not student learning. From there, participants audit their existing assignments, anchor each to its underlying human-centric learning objective, and use the Studio’s interactive toolkit to rebuild around process, context, and verification.

What Faculty Can Do Now

The Studio is designed for incremental implementation. Three starting points any instructor can act on immediately:

Add one process checkpoint to an existing assignment. Ask students to submit a prompt history or a brief reflection log alongside their final draft. This alone shifts the locus of accountability.

Introduce one locally-grounded or experiential activity per unit. Field observations, community interviews, and maker projects are inherently AI-resistant because they require physical presence and specific context.

Replace a detection-focused policy with a disclosure-focused one. Shift from “prove you didn’t use AI” to “show me how you used AI and what you did with its output.”

Reclaiming the Classroom as a Human Space

The goal of AI-resistant pedagogy is not to win an arms race with technology. It is to reclaim the classroom as a space where the process of learning is just as valuable as the final product. By focusing on intentional design, critical empathy, and equitable access, we can build courses where AI becomes a legitimate collaborator in learning—not a shortcut around it.

The full Studio, including its interactive assignment redesign toolkit, case studies, and downloadable resources, is freely available at https://ynaqbxzy.manus.space/. It is a practitioner-first resource built to reduce manual instructional labor while strengthening the human core of every course.

Stacy Ybarra Evans, EdD, is a San Antonio-based educator and instructional strategist specializing in the integration of emerging technologies and AI-resistant pedagogy within higher education. She currently serves on the SXSW EDU 2026 Advisory Board and the Macmillan Accessibility Advisory Board, where she helps shape the future of educational content and inclusivity. Her approach focuses on bridging the gap between rapidly evolving generative AI tools and traditional learning objectives to ensure authentic student engagement. Her expertise is further grounded in her role as a Quality Matters Master Reviewer, ensuring that innovative course design meets the highest national standards for digital learning and academic integrity.
